paras: The attempted lynching of John Hunter was a failed attack by a masked mob on the jail at Washington, Daviess County, Indiana, in the night of September 9-10, 1882, to seize and lynch Hunter, who was held for the killing of William Lentz. An armed guard placed by the sheriff held the jail, and the mob dispersed after appeals from the sheriff and the prosecuting attorney. The story ran as a telegraphic brief across the country, and Hunter was later convicted at Vincennes and sentenced to hang.

According to an August 18 dispatch, Hunter shot and killed William Lents, a 28-year-old farmer, at a picnic seven miles from town after interfering in a fight between Lents' brother and a man named Hawes. The same report said Hunter, who was keeping a lemonade stand at the picnic, had just returned from a prison term for the killing of Hiram Wykoff three years earlier. That dispatch carried a 'Washington, Mo.' dateline, but its names and setting match the Indiana case, and a later brief placed the killing in Daviess County, Indiana.
Learning that a mob planned to take Hunter from jail, the sheriff secretly garrisoned the building with armed men, thirty by most counts and twelve by one.

A Chicago Times special said a masked mob 'from the country' gathered early on Sunday morning, displaced the ropes of the fire and police bells and fired volleys to frighten the townspeople. About fifty men then went over the jail fence and made three attempts to force the doors, all of which failed. A weekly digest added that the mob seized the sheriff and searched him for the cell keys, which they did not find, before the guard drove them off.

A dispatch from Washington identified the men as relatives of the Wykoff and Lentz families, which had 'suffered from Hunter's unerring aim'. The sheriff and prosecuting attorney persuaded them to leave, while Hunter, in the papers' words, 'crouched low in his cell'. The men did not give up, according to that report, and threatened to storm the jail unless Hunter was tried and convicted that week, so the guard stayed in place.

No report of arrests or charges against members of the mob was found in the coverage. In November a jury at Vincennes convicted Hunter of murdering Lentz, and he was said to have remarked in court that he had already killed three men and would die content if he could kill three more. The same brief said that after the killing he fled to Paris, Illinois, and that his uncle bargained with the sheriff to surrender him for $50. A Missouri paper reported at the end of November that Hunter had been sentenced to be hanged; no report of the execution was found.

White papers from Washington, D.C., New York, Memphis, Sacramento, Dakota Territory and Nevada carried the story on September 11 and 12 under headlines such as 'A Jail Besieged by Lynchers', 'Unsuccessful Attempt at Lynching' and 'Wanting to Lynch a Prisoner'. The Memphis Public Ledger printed two versions in one issue, one of them headed 'The Kuklux in Indiana' although its text spoke only of masked men. Weekly roundups in Ohio, Tennessee, Arkansas and Missouri reprinted the masked-mob item into late September, some dating it only to 'the other morning'.

Every version called Hunter a murderer before his trial and described the mob as 'vigilantes' or 'desperate men' without editorial comment. None of the reports gave the race of Hunter or of the men who attacked the jail.

Reports disagree on the timing: several place the attack at midnight on Saturday or the night of the 9th, the Chicago Times special says early Sunday, and a September 11 dispatch says 2 o'clock 'this morning'. The guard numbered thirty in the longer dispatches and twelve in the midnight-Saturday brief, and only the digest account reports the seizure of the sheriff.

bases: Masked men tried to take John Hunter, held for the killing of William Lentz, from the Washington, Indiana, jail to lynch him and were turned back by guards (A5, A7, A19).

A mob of about fifty masked men acting without authority tried to seize and lynch Hunter for an alleged murder, but no one was killed; Hunter stayed in his cell and was later tried and sentenced to hang (A5, A19, A38). It was an attempted lynching.
Separate dispatches (the Chicago Times special, the Washington, Ind., relatives dispatch and the midnight-Saturday brief) independently report the failed attack on the jail (A5, A7, A8).

accounts.label: Chicago Times special
accounts.gist: A masked mob from the country gathered early on the morning of September 10, disabled the alarm bells, fired volleys and sent fifty men over the fence, but three attempts on the doors failed and the sheriff's and prosecutor's appeals dispersed it.

accounts.label: Washington, Ind., special of September 11
accounts.gist: Relatives of the Wykoff and Lentz families came to the jail at 2 o'clock, could not force it and were talked out of trouble, but threatened to storm it unless Hunter was tried and convicted that week.

accounts.label: Midnight-Saturday brief
accounts.gist: Masked men tried at midnight on Saturday to take Hunter from jail and lynch him and were repulsed by twelve armed men.

accounts.label: Weekly digest account
accounts.gist: About fifty masked men surrounded the jail on the night of the 9th, seized the sheriff and searched him for the cell keys, then were repulsed by the guard when they tried to break in.

framing.detail: Brief telegraphic items called Hunter 'the murderer' and the mob 'vigilantes' or 'desperate men', without editorial comment on the attempt.
The Memphis Public Ledger headed its midnight-Saturday brief 'The Kuklux in Indiana', though the text described only masked men.
